1: [Gita 2:12-13 — The Self that does not die]

Never was there a time when I was not, nor you, nor these lords of men; nor will there ever be a time when we shall cease to be, all of us, hereafter. As the soul passes in this body through childhood, youth, and age, so too it passes into another body; the wise are not confused by this.

He is never born, and He never dies; He has never come to be, and He will never cease to be. Unborn, eternal, abiding, ancient — He is not slain when the body is slain. Weapons do not cut Him, fire does not burn Him, water does not wet Him, wind does not dry Him.
[Gita 2:47 — The right to the work alone]

Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Let not the fruits of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. Established in yoga, perform action, abandoning attachment, even-minded in success and failure — for evenness of mind is called yoga.
2: Whenever righteousness decays and unrighteousness prevails, then I manifest Myself, O Bharata. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of evil, and for the firm establishment of righteousness, I am born from age to age.

The wise see with an equal eye a learned and humble brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a dog-eater. Those whose minds are established in equality have already conquered the world here itself — for God is perfect and equal, and they who stand in His likeness stand in God.

Let a man lift himself by himself; let him not degrade himself. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self. The self is the friend of him who has conquered himself; but for him who has not, the self remains his own enemy, standing against him like a stranger.
3: To those who worship Me with undivided devotion, meditating on Me, I carry what they lack, and I preserve what they have. Those who worship other gods with faith worship Me alone, O son of Kunti, though by a mistaken way — for I alone am the enjoyer of all sacrifice, and the Lord of all the worlds.

Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water — that offering of love, from the striving soul, I accept. Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer, whatever you give, whatever penance you practise — do it all as an offering to Me.

He who hates no creature, who is friendly and compassionate to all, who is free from the thought of 'mine' and from ego, even-minded in pain and pleasure, forgiving, ever content, steady in meditation, self-controlled, firm in his resolve — he who is thus devoted to Me, he is dear to Me.
